Spratelloides lewisi is a small, short-lived clupeoid fish native to the tropical Indo-Pacific. This species exhibits a modest maximum body size, with adults attaining an ultimate standard length of 6 centimeters [Li = 6 centimeters], a dimension typical of many small planktivorous forage fishes in coral reef ecosystems. Hatchlings emerge from pelagic eggs at an extremely small size; the wet weight at birth has been calculated at 0.000048 grams [Wwb = 0.000048 grams], a value derived from the egg diameter of the closely related congener Spratelloides gracilis. This minuscule neonatal mass imposes substantial constraints on early life survival, as the yolk-sac larva must rapidly develop functional feeding structures to transition to exogenous nutrition before exhausting its endogenous reserves. The subsequent growth trajectory is rapid, allowing individuals to attain sizes sufficient for reproduction within their abbreviated life cycle. Comparative studies within the genus indicate that the standard length at puberty is approximately 2.3 centimeters [Lp = approximately 2.3 centimeters].

Sexual maturation in Spratelloides lewisi begins relatively early in the life span. Puberty, defined by the onset of gametogenesis and vitellogenesis, occurs when individuals reach a standard length of approximately 2.3 centimeters [Lp = approximately 2.3 centimeters], a size that represents roughly 38 percent of the ultimate standard length of 6 centimeters [Li = 6 centimeters]. This proportional size at maturation is similar to that observed in Spratelloides gracilis, where puberty occurs at about 38 percent of its asymptotic length. The timing of this developmental milestone is presumably linked to the accumulation of sufficient somatic tissue to support the energetic demands of gonadal recrudescence and subsequent spawning activity. Once mature, the reproductively active adult enters a phase of frequent spawning. Under optimal environmental conditions at 28.8 °C [T = 28.8 °C], females are capable of a high maximum reproductive rate, releasing approximately 4.8 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 4.8 eggs per day], a considerable daily fecundity for a fish of this diminutive size.

At the stable water temperature of 28.8 °C [T = 28.8 °C], which represents typical tropical surface conditions within the species' range, the life cycle of Spratelloides lewisi proceeds with notable brevity. The maximum lifespan has been recorded as approximately 183 days [am = approximately 183 days], a remarkably short duration that constrains the species to a single, intense reproductive window at a temperature of 28.8 °C [T = 28.8 °C]. This life span of roughly 6 months is consistent with the extreme r-selected life-history strategy observed in many small, ephemeral clupeoids. The rapid pace of life is further emphasized by the early attainment of sexual maturation: individuals reach the standard length at puberty of approximately 2.3 centimeters [Lp = approximately 2.3 centimeters] within a few weeks of hatching, allowing them to commence spawning activities almost immediately after completing somatic growth. This compressed schedule necessitates a high daily investment in reproduction. Under the same thermal regime, females achieve a maximum reproductive rate of roughly 4.8 eggs per day [Ri = roughly 4.8 eggs per day].

The ultimate wet weight of Spratelloides lewisi, a key parameter defining its maximum somatic investment, has been estimated at 1.43 grams [Wwi = 1.43 grams]. This value, derived from a length-weight regression using a species-based length exponent common among small clupeiforms, places the adult body mass well within the typical range for forage fish of similar standard length. For a fish with an ultimate standard length of 6 centimeters [Li = 6 centimeters], this mass reflects a moderately fusiform body shape and a relatively low condition factor. The contrast between the tiny wet weight at birth of 0.000048 grams [Wwb = 0.000048 grams] and the ultimate wet weight of 1.43 grams [Wwi = 1.43 grams] reveals an astonishing mass increase of nearly 30,000-fold over the course of development. Such a dramatic growth trajectory is typical of teleosts that begin life as a minute pelagic egg and must quickly reach a size capable of exploiting the rich zooplankton resources of the epipelagic zone.

Within the bathypelagic and epipelagic strata it inhabits, the lifespan of Spratelloides lewisi is tightly coupled to the seasonal availability of its zooplankton prey. The maximum lifespan of approximately 183 days [am = approximately 183 days], as estimated under laboratory conditions at 28.8 °C [T = 28.8 °C], aligns with a single monsoon-driven productivity pulse in many parts of its range. This ephemeral existence is a classic example of a semelparous or near-semelparous life history among small tropical clupeoids. Despite its abbreviated life cycle, the species achieves considerable annual reproductive output through its exceptionally high daily fecundity: with a daily reproductive rate of roughly 4.8 eggs per day [Ri = roughly 4.8 eggs per day] at 28.8 °C [T = 28.8 °C], and a reproductive window spanning several weeks, the total lifetime fecundity is substantial. The ultimate wet weight of 1.43 grams [Wwi = 1.43 grams] thus supports a prodigious allocation of resources to reproduction.
